n: After the Sabbath, at dawn on Sunday, Mary Magdalene and the other Mary come to see the tomb. Sunday became the Lord’s Day because of this morning.

f.w: the first day of the week

f.g: Probably Mary the mother of James and Joses.

n: A great earthquake strikes as an angel of the Lord descends, rolls the stone away, and sits on it. The stone is moved not to let Jesus out, but to let witnesses in.
The angel’s appearance blazes like lightning, his clothing white as snow — the brilliance of heavenly glory.
The guards shake with fear and collapse like dead men. The soldiers posted to keep a dead man in look dead themselves.
The angel comforts the women: don’t be afraid. He knows they are looking for Jesus who was crucified.
The central declaration of the Christian faith: “He is not here: for he is risen, as he said.” The women are invited to see the empty place for themselves.

f.w: he is risen, as he said
Come, see the place where the Lord lay

n: They are sent to tell the disciples that Jesus has risen and will meet them in Galilee. These women become the first messengers of the Resurrection.

f.w: he goeth before you into Galilee

n: They hurry from the tomb, filled with both fear and great joy, running to tell the disciples.

f.g: Awe and joy together — a natural response to the holy.

n: On the way, the risen Jesus himself meets them. They grasp his feet and worship him — touching a real, physical, resurrected body.
Jesus repeats the message, tenderly calling the disciples who abandoned him “my brethren.” He has not given up on them.
Meanwhile some of the guards report everything to the chief priests.
The leaders meet and decide to bribe the soldiers with a large sum of money.

f.g: A large amount of silver — ironically paid again to suppress the truth about Jesus.

n: The cover story: the disciples stole the body while the guards slept. It is a weak story — how would sleeping guards know who took it?

f.w: stole him away while we slept

n: Sleeping on duty could mean death for a Roman soldier, so the leaders promise to protect them if Pilate hears.
The soldiers take the money and spread the story, which Matthew says was still circulating when he wrote.

f.g: Until the time Matthew wrote his Gospel, likely a few decades later.

n: The eleven apostles — Judas is gone — go to the mountain in Galilee where Jesus told them to meet him.

f.g: Mountains frame Jesus’s ministry in Matthew: temptation, sermon, transfiguration, and now commission.

n: When they see him they worship him, though some hesitate. Matthew honestly records that faith sometimes grows gradually.

f.g: Greek distazō — to waver or hesitate, the word used of Peter on the water.

n: Jesus comes near and declares that all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to him.

f.w: All power is given unto me

n: The Great Commission: go to all nations — no longer only Israel — making disciples and baptizing them in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Ghost.

f.w: baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost

n: They must teach people to live all he has commanded. Matthew ends with a promise: “I am with you always.” The Gospel that began with “God with us” ends with Christ remaining with his disciples.

f.g: The end of the age — the JST and JS—Matthew render similar phrases as “the destruction of the wicked.”
